entries.boundary: The stop-path fix is verified only on the NullRHI gate; the GB10 path could not be re-run. The Shutdown field is best effort: the status is exact but ambiguous, because UE's graceful handler exits with 128+signal and so does an unhandled kill, and the log that separates them is truncated mid-write by the very crash under investigation, so the status takes precedence and the log only upgrades the verdict. A trial engine change that installed the Unix termination handler was reverted: it produced no observable difference and an unproven engine divergence is worse than none. The shutdown crash itself is located but not fixed: RemoveHandler is reached only from FSocket::Reset (a move-only type, so no double unregister by copy), the registrars are the LightGrid, Nanite and VirtualShadowMap status-feedback sockets, and the log shows the check failure triggering UE's forced exit immediately before the SIGSEGV, so the signal is likely a by-product of that path rather than evidence of memory corruption in GPU messaging.

entries.change: Add probe-ue-shutdown-crash.sh, dump-ue-shutdown.gdb, gdb_ue_shutdown_capture.py and analyze_ue_shutdown_capture.py plus `make carla-ue-shutdown-crash` to capture the first failed check on the NullRHI shutdown path. The inferior is discovered through /proc/<gdb pid>/task/*/children and verified against the binary's exe target before any signal is sent, shutdown is requested with SIGTERM to the inferior once the RPC world answers, and the capture records the check hook, the socket register/remove ledger, the handler map state and the ABI argument registers. It also instruments both release paths (GPUMessage::FSystem::ReleaseRHI and Nanite::FGlobalResources::ReleaseRHI) and stamps a single monotonic `order` on every observation, with the handler map's size recorded at each one, so the run reads as one timeline. It also marks the exit boundary (a breakpoint on exit, kept pending because libc is not mapped when the breakpoints are created) so each release can be attributed to a teardown phase, and reports release_phases next to the ordered timeline.
entries.reason: The shutdown crash at GPUMessaging.cpp:68 had never been caught in the act: the log stops at Signal 11, core files go to an apport helper that is absent in the container, and two hand-run gdb attempts failed (pgrep -f matched the probe's own command line and killed PID 1; `break FSystem::RemoveHandler` does not resolve because the class lives in namespace GPUMessage). A write watchpoint on GPUMessage::GSystem.MessageHandlers.Pairs.Elements.Data.ArrayNum fires twice: at the registration the map goes 0->1 from TMapBase::Emplace, and at order 5 it goes 1->0 from ~TMapBase <- GPUMessage::FSystem::~FSystem on libc's exit() static-destruction path, three observations before the failed check at order 8. Nanite::FGlobalResources::ReleaseRHI then runs delete FeedbackManager (NaniteShared.cpp:309), so ~FSocket -> FSocket::Reset -> RemoveHandler(0) asserts against a destroyed map and the following TMap::Remove touches freed storage. Under gdb the same run ends with no signal at all and exit 143, confirming that the wild 139 comes from the non-debugger fatal path. The release instrumentation settled an open question: FSystem::ReleaseRHI runs at order 5 while the map still holds its one handler, so it passes cleanly and does not clear the map, while Nanite's ReleaseRHI runs at order 7 with the map already empty. Both enter from FRenderResource::ReleaseResource; the caller of that function is still unmeasured because gdb's unwind stops at that frame in this build. The exit marker attributed both releases to inside-exit-handlers, so neither is an explicit release during RHI shutdown: the defect is purely the relative order of the two TGlobalResource destructors, whose destructor body calls the release before the resource's members are destroyed (RenderResource.h:568). That also corrected an earlier draft inference in the report, which had read the release-before-members order as evidence of an explicit call. Installing the marker exposed an instrument defect as well: the installer deleted any breakpoint that did not resolve at creation, which is right for the binary's own symbols but silently dropped a libc symbol; such roles now stay pending and their binding is read back after the run.

entries.boundary: A debugger makes FPlatformMisc::IsDebuggerPresent() true, so CheckVerifyFailedImpl2 skips AssertFailedImplV and the caller runs PLATFORM_BREAK() instead of the fatal path. This capture is evidence about the failed invariant, its id, its caller and the ordering of the map destruction, not about the exit status; it says nothing about the exit code 139 recorded on stock runs. The probe has been exercised on NullRHI only, and no engine-side fix has been made: making FSocket::Reset() tolerate a released manager, or giving GSystem a longer lifetime, is an upstream decision that would affect every GPU message user.

entries.change: Add an unapplied engine patch proposal, scripts/carla/patches/ue-gpumessaging-shutdown-guard.patch, that gives GPUMessage::FSystem a destructor setting bIsBeingDestroyed before its members are destroyed and makes GPUMessage::FSocket::Reset() skip the unregister while that flag is set. It touches one file, adds no includes, and is documented as a third patch category in scripts/carla/patches/README.md. The hand-off form is the bundle under artifacts/ue-gpumessaging-shutdown/20261003T062016Z/ (report.md, COVER-NOTE.md and the capture it cites), which is not tracked.
entries.reason: The map write watchpoint showed the handler map going 1->0 at order 5, three observations before the failed check at order 8, with the stack running ~TMapBase <- GPUMessage::FSystem::~FSystem <- libc's exit() static-destruction path. Because both GSystem and Nanite::FGlobalResources are TGlobalResource globals, ~FSocket can run after the manager it unregisters into, so RemoveHandler asserts on a destroyed map and the following TMap::Remove touches freed storage. The proposed guard fixes the shared unregister path for every socket owner without relaxing the assertion itself, which still catches genuine double-unregister bugs. Applying it is an upstream decision that would affect every GPU message user, so it is recorded as a proposal rather than applied.
